title: Breed Rankings
text:
The Breed Rank data gives information about different types of breek ranks. The specific dataset called breed_rank_all gives information about the ranking of each dog breed recorded from the years 2013 to 2020. There are 195 different types of breeds that this data set contains.
This data set is a Breed Rankings Dataset from Kkakey courtesy of American Kennel Club. This data has been made available by KKakey through the TidyTuesday Data Link

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

breed_rank_all <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2022/2022-02-01/breed_rank.csv')


ggplot(breed_rank_all, aes(x = `2013 Rank`, y = `2020 Rank`)) + 
    geom_point() +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
    labs(title = "Dog Breed Rankings 2013 vs 2020" )








The graph compares the dog breed rankings from the year 2013 to the year 2020. The red slope line attemps to highlight how the ranking between each year doesn’t change much. It would be interesting to learn more about which specific breeds are farther away from this trendline.

title: Simpson Episodes
text:
This data set analyzes the episodes from the TV show The Simpsons. Episodes and script lines have been filtered to only include episodes from 2010 to 2016. The data contains information about the imdb rating, voting, number in the series, season, title, views, and more.
This dataset is a Simpsons Dataset from Kaggle which was made available to the public by Prashant Banerjee. Thank you to Nicolas Foss, Ed.D., MS with Iowa HHS who curated the data set in linked in TidyTuesday

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

simpsons_episodes <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-02-04/simpsons_episodes.csv')


ggplot(simpsons_episodes, aes(x = views, y = imdb_rating)) + 
    geom_point() +
    labs(title = "Rating vs Views of Simpsons Episodes" )








The graph compares the imdb rating to the views of each Simpson episode within the data set. While most of the data points are skewed to the right side, there are a handful of episodes that have 0 or close to 0 views, yet relatively good ratings. Overall, the greater the number of views, the greater the rating is.

title: The Office Quotes
text:
This data set has information on all of the lines spoken in the American sitcom show, The Office. The data set tracks all lines from all 9 seasons and includes the season, episode, line, character who spoke the line, and what number line it was in the entire show. In total there are 61,306 lines!
This dataset has been created by Kaggle and was originally scraped from a website called Office Quotes that is currently down.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

office_lines <- read.csv("the-office_lines.csv")



The code below gives you a ranking of each character, calculating the length of lines for each character from The Office. I calculated the length of each line for each character and the summed up the length of all of their lines.



Code
office_lines_changed <- office_lines |>
  group_by(Character) |>
  mutate(line_length = str_length(Line))|>
  summarize(total_length = sum(line_length, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(total_length)) |>
  head(10)




One of the most common phrases that is repeated in The Office is “That’s what she said.” The main character Michael often repeats this innapropriate joke and I wanted to count how many times this joke was repeated by each character. First I found it helpful to change each string to all lower case and then use a regular expression brackets to choose either a straight or curly apostrophe.



Code
office_lines |>
  mutate(Line = str_to_lower(Line))|>
  group_by(Character) |>
  summarize(exclaim_counter = sum(str_count(Line, "that['’]s what she said")))|>
  arrange(desc(exclaim_counter))

One of my favorite characters is Dwight Schrute. He is known as one of the most comedic characters in the show. Using lookarounds, I wrote code to see what the characters talk about when he is mentioned. Some examples are shown below.

  mutate(Character = fct_lump(Character, n = 5, w = total_length))

  mutate(Character = fct_reorder(Character, total_length, .desc = TRUE))

ggplot(office_lines_changed, aes(x = Character, y = total_length, fill = Character))+
  geom_col() +

    title = "Total Length of Lines of Characters in The Office"

PLOT 1: Length of Lines of Characters in The Office If you wanted to see how big of a role each character has in The Office throughout all 9 seasons, one way to track this could be to calculate the length of their lines. This plot above calculates the total length of all of each characters lines in terms of the physical length of each word in their lines. From this plot we can see that Michael, the main character, speaks the most. I was surprised to see that Andy spoke more than Pam because I always thought Pam was one of the more prevelant characters in the show. The pink other column represents all of the other characters in the show who had smaller roles. Some of those characters include Kevin, Angela, Phyllis, and more.




Code
office_lines_dwight <- office_lines |>
  group_by(Season) |>
  summarize(dwight_string = sum(str_detect(Line, "Dwight"))) 

ggplot(office_lines_dwight, aes(x = Season, y = dwight_string, fill = Season))+
  geom_col()+
  labs(
    y = "'Dwight' Mentions",
    title = "How Often is 'Dwight' Mentioned in Each Season?"

PLOT 2: How Often is Dwight Mentioned in Each Season?

Using concept of tracking the times Dwight is mentioned in the Office, I plotted how many times Dwight is mentioned in each season. This gives us insight to how often the other characters talk about Dwight each season. With this data we can see that generally over time his popularity in the show increases. Although in season 2 and 3 Dwight is mentioned a lot more than in Season 4, 6, and 7. It would be interested to compare the data of all of the other characters and see which seasons highlight individual plots for each character. Maybe Dwight is mentioned less in Season 4 because Jim and Pam start dating then and are mentioned more by other characters.

title: Air Quality
text:
The UK Weather data set explores climate data such as mean daily minimum and maximum temperatures, total rainfall, total sunshine hours and days of frost for each month in each year starting from 1941. The Historic UK Meteorological & Climate Data has been provided by the UK Met Office which is the national weather service in the UK. Thank you to Jack Davison who scraped the data and published it to Tidy Tuesday


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

UK_weather <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-10-21/historic_station_met.csv')


In the UK, the summers are often warm, however within the past few years there have been record high temperatures during the month of July. I thought it would be interesting to uncover the data from the month of July from an earlier range of years to a later range.

title: UK Weather
text:
The UK Weather data set explores climate data such as mean daily minimum and maximum temperatures, total rainfall, total sunshine hours and days of frost for each month in each year from 1930s to 2024. The Historic UK Meteorological & Climate Data has been provided by the UK Met Office which is the national weather service in the UK. Thank you to Jack Davison who scraped the data and published it to Tidy Tuesday


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

uk_weather <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-10-21/historic_station_met.csv')


In the UK, the weather is varied: some months bring very high temperatures, while others are cold. July is known to be one of the months whose weather has changed the most over the years. Using weather data from the 1940s to the 2020s from several weather stations around the UK, I hope to compare rainfall with maximum temperature in July of each year. Rain can occur at both low and high temperatures, how can we begin to understand this relationship?
My research question: Is there a correlation between maximum temperature and total rainfall in July?
To understand this question, I have chosen to focus on two stations: Heathrow and Lerwick. Heathrow is a station that is not far from central London, whereas Lerwick is the most northern station in the UK. I thought it would be interesting to compare the data of these two stations.

title: UK Weather
text:
Station Heathrow

Welcome to Heathrow!
If you are traveling to London, England you might land in London Heathrow Airport. It is one of the world’s busiest aviation hubs. Fun Fact! Did you know that there is in fact a secret terminal called The Windsor where only royal family members, diplomats, and VIP flyers can take off from?
From the data in the UK weather dataset, here is the scatterplot that helps us understand how rainfall and maximum temperature in the month of July are possibly related.


Code
heathrow_july <- uk_weather |>
  filter(station == "heathrow", month == 7) |>
  select(station, month, year, tmax, rain) 

ggplot(heathrow_july, aes(x = tmax, y = rain))+
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Heathrow Rainfall vs Max Temperature in July 1948-2024",
    x = "Maximum Temperature (°C)", 
    y = "Rainfall (mm)", 
    caption = "Figure 1"
    ) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)) 









Figure 1 illustrates the relationship between maximum temperature in July and rainfall at the Heathrow Station. The general trend shows that as the maximum temperature increases, the rainfall decreases.


Code
correlation_heathrow <- heathrow_july |>
  summarize(r = cor(tmax, rain)) |>
  pull(r)
cat("The calculated correlation between rainfall and maximum temperature at Heathrow station is: ", correlation_heathrow)


The calculated correlation between rainfall and maximum temperature at Heathrow station is:  -0.482847

Using weather data from the 1940s to the 2020s from several weather stations around the UK, I hope to compare rainfall with maximum temperature in July of each year. My research question: Is there a correlation between maximum temperature and total rainfall in July?

text:
Applying Shuffling to Heathrow Data


Code
set.seed(47)
shuffle_plot <- shuffle_points(1, heathrow_july)

ggplot(shuffle_plot, aes(x = shuffle_temp, y = rain)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Heathrow Rainfall vs. Shuffled Max \n Temperature",
    x = "Shuffled Max Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Rainfall (mm)"
  )











Code
set.seed(47)
shuffled_heathrow <- map(1:1000, shuffle_correlation, dataframe = heathrow_july)|>
list_rbind()

shuffled_heathrow |>
  ggplot(aes(x = correlation)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = correlation_heathrow, color = "red", linewidth = 1)+
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = correlation_heathrow,
    y = Inf,
    label = paste("observed r =", round(correlation_heathrow, 3)),
    color = "red",
    hjust = -0.05,
    vjust = 1.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation of Shuffled Temperature \n vs Rainfall at Heathrow", 
    x = "Temperature and Rainfall Correlation",
    y = "Number of Shuffles"
  )

title: UK Weather
text:
Lerwick Station
While Heathrow Station resides just outside of central London, Lerwick is the most northern meteorological station in the UK. As a result, I wondered if the correlation between maximum temperature and rainfall in July would be any different.


Code
lerwick_july <- uk_weather |>
  filter(station == "lerwick", month == 7) |>
  select(station, month, year, tmax, rain)

ggplot(lerwick_july, aes(x = tmax, y = rain))+
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Lerwick Rainfall vs Max Temperature in July 1931-2024", 
    x = "Maximum Temperature (°C)", 
    y = "Rainfall (mm)", 
    caption = "Figure 4"
    )+ 
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)) 









Figure 4 above shows a plot of the maximum temperatures during July vs the rainfall measured at Lerwick Station. In comparison to Figure 1 (Heathrow Station), the dots are more scattered and don’t follow a general trend.


Code
correlation_lerwick <- lerwick_july |>
  summarize(r = cor(tmax, rain)) |>
  pull(r)
cat("The calculated correlation between rainfall and maximum temperature at Lerwick station is: ", correlation_lerwick)


The calculated correlation between rainfall and maximum temperature at Lerwick station is:  -0.05910021

section: Applying Hypothesis Testing to Heathrow Data
text:
Applying Hypothesis Testing to Heathrow Data


Code
set.seed(47)
shuffle_plot_heathrow <- shuffle_points(1, heathrow_july)

ggplot(shuffle_plot_heathrow, aes(x = shuffle_temp, y = rain)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Heathrow Rainfall vs. Shuffled Max Temperature",
    x = "Shuffled Max Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Rainfall (mm)", 
    caption = "Figure 2"
  ) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)) 









Figure 2 represents the shuffled maximum temperatures vs the rainfall when the temperatures are shuffled once. In simple terms, this means that the assigned maximum temperatures have been shuffled randomly. In the graph above we can see that the shuffled temperatures don’t have a similar negative correlation as the original graph. To understand more we need to map the shuffle function multiple times. By mapping we are iterating this shuffling correlation function a thousand times which will give us lots of data points.


Code
set.seed(47)
shuffled_heathrow <- map(1:1000, shuffle_correlation, dataframe = heathrow_july)|>
list_rbind()   

shuffled_heathrow |>
  ggplot(aes(x = correlation)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = correlation_heathrow, color = "red", linewidth = 1)+
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = correlation_heathrow,
    y = Inf,
    label = paste("observed r =", round(correlation_heathrow, 3)),
    color = "red",
    hjust = -0.05,
    vjust = 1.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation of Shuffled Temperature vs Rainfall at Heathrow", 
    x = "Temperature and Rainfall Correlation",
    y = "Number of Shuffles", 
    caption = "Figure 3"
  ) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)) 









Figure 3 represents the mapped correlation values for rainfall and maximum temperature in July at Heathrow Station. The mapping line of code applies the shuffle_correlation function a thousand times which shuffles the temperatures a thousand times and then spits out 1 correlation value for each shuffle. As we can see, the red line to the left of the histogram is far from the correlation values. The red line represents the original observed correlation value which was calculated to be -0.483. Since the correlation is far from the correlation calculated by the random shuffling temperature, we can make the conclusion that there is a negative correlation: As maximum temperature increases in July, the rainfall decreases.

P-Value


Code
shuffled_heathrow |>
  summarize(p_value = mean(abs(correlation) >= abs(correlation_heathrow)))


# A tibble: 1 × 1
  p_value
    <dbl>
1       0


The p-value calculated above supports the previous statement that we reject the null hypothesis. Therefore the observed data did not happen just by chance or randomness.

title: UK Weather
text:
Applying Shuffling to Lerwick Data
Again, to begin our investigation of the correlation between rainfall and maximum temperature we need to test the null hypothesis. The null hypothesis is the test that there is no relationship between these two variables. We are testing if the values of rainfall and maximum temperature happen just by random chance.


Code
set.seed(123)
shuffle_plot_lerwick <- shuffle_points(1, lerwick_july)

ggplot(shuffle_plot_lerwick, aes(x = shuffle_temp, y = rain)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Lerwick Rainfall vs. Shuffled Max Temperature",
    x = "Shuffled Max Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Rainfall (mm)", 
    caption = "Figure 5"
  ) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)) 









Similar to Figure 2, Figure 5 illustrates the shuffled maximum temperatures vs rainfall in Lerwick Station when the temperatures were shuffled once. However, to investigate the null hypothesis we map the shuffle function of the lerwick data multiple times.


Code
set.seed(47)
shuffled_lerwick <- map(1:1000, shuffle_correlation, dataframe = lerwick_july)|>
list_rbind()

shuffled_lerwick |>
  ggplot(aes(x = correlation)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = correlation_lerwick, color = "red", linewidth = 1)+
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = correlation_lerwick,
    y = Inf,
    label = paste("observed r =", round(correlation_lerwick, 3)),
    color = "red",
    hjust = -0.05,
    vjust = 1.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation of Shuffled Temperature vs Rainfall at Lerwick", 
    x = "Temperature and Rainfall Correlation",
    y = "Number of Shuffles", 
    caption = "Figure 6"
  )+
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)) 









While the process of mapping and iterating the shuffle function was similar to the Heathrow Data, Figure 6 illustrates how the relationship between temperature and rainfall was different in the two stations. The red correlation value which is -0.059 overlaps with correlation of shuffled temperatures vs rainfall. Unlike Figure 3, we are unable to make the conclusion that there is a distinct relationship between rainfall and maximum temperature because the correlation falls in the region where randomness could have occurred. Not only does it fall in the region, but it is less than 0.1 off of the most central and peak part of the graph. Since the correlation values falls in this region, we need more information/cannot make a conclusion that these two variables depend on each other directly.

P-Value


Code
shuffled_lerwick |>
  summarize(p_value = mean(abs(correlation) >= abs(correlation_lerwick)))


# A tibble: 1 × 1
  p_value
    <dbl>
1   0.548


According to statistics, if the p value is greater than a value of 0.05, then that data fails to reject the null hypothesis. In this scenario the value of the p value calculated above is 0.548 which is a lot greater than 0.05, and there we cannot reject the idea of randomness.
